notes.meaning: The Lord gave Moses rules for when someone committed deliberate wrongs against a neighbor, such as keeping a stolen item, cheating in a business deal, or lying under oath about lost property. Even though these crimes hurt other people, God counted them as direct unfaithfulness against Himself. Harming another person breaks the trust God designed for community life and dishonors His name.

When guilty people realized their sin and confessed, they had to return everything they had stolen, kept, or gained by fraud. They also had to add an extra twenty percent of the value to make up for the owner's loss during that time. God required wrongdoers to make things right with the person they hurt before they could seek peace with Him.

After paying back the victim in full, the offender brought an unblemished ram of proper value to the priest as a guilt offering. The priest offered it to make atonement—a sacrifice that covered the wrongdoing and restored friendship with God—and the person was fully forgiven. This demonstrated that sincere confession, restitution, and sacrifice brought real pardon even for intentional sins.

God directed Moses to give specific instructions to Aaron and his sons about caring for the daily burnt offering. The sacrifice was placed on the altar hearth to burn slowly all through the night until the morning. This steady burning showed that God's people were constantly devoted to Him and remained under His care day and night.

Each morning, the priest put on his special linen robe and undergarments to clear the ashes off the altar and place them beside it. Afterwards, he changed into other clothes and carried the ashes outside the camp to a ceremonially clean location. Treating the ashes with care showed deep reverence for holy things in God's presence.

The fire on the bronze altar was to be kept burning continuously and never allowed to go out. The priest added fresh firewood every morning, laid out the burnt offering, and burned the fat of the peace offerings upon it. This unbroken flame reminded the nation of God's constant presence and called them to keep their own love and prayers burning without stopping.

When an Israelite presented a grain offering, the priests brought it before the Lord at the front of the altar. The officiating priest took a handful of the fine flour, olive oil, and all the frankincense to burn as a memorial portion that smelled pleasing to the Lord. The rest of the flour was reserved to feed the priests who served God full-time.

Aaron and his sons were instructed to bake the remaining flour without yeast and eat it within the courtyard of the tabernacle. Because this food was most holy, only male priests were allowed to eat it, serving as their regular food since they held no tribal farmland. In addition, whatever touched these holy gifts had to be treated with special reverence.

When the high priest was anointed, he brought a grain offering of about two quarts of fine flour. Half was prepared on a griddle with oil and offered in the morning, and the remaining half was brought in the evening. It was broken into pieces and presented on the altar as a pleasing aroma, dedicating the priest's service to God.

Every high priest who succeeded Aaron was required to present this grain offering, and it had to be burned entirely on the altar. When priests sacrificed for ordinary people, they were allowed to eat part of the food, but their own grain offerings could never be eaten. This showed that priests could not make a profit from their own offerings or bear their own guilt before God.

God gave regulations for the sin offering of regular worshippers, ordering the animal to be slaughtered on the north side of the altar where the burnt offering was killed. The priest who conducted the service was to eat the meat in the holy courtyard of the tent of meeting. Eating this portion provided nourishment for the priest and symbolized his role in helping carry the sins of the community.

The sin offering was so sacred that any blood splashed onto clothing had to be washed out right away in the sacred courtyard. Clay pots used to boil the meat had to be broken because the broth soaked into the porous clay, while bronze pots could be scrubbed clean and rinsed. These rules ensured that items marked by holy sacrifices were never mixed back into everyday household chores.

Any male from the priestly families was permitted to eat the meat of an ordinary sin offering within the tabernacle grounds. However, if the blood of a sin offering had been brought inside the Holy Place to make atonement for the high priest or the whole nation, none of the meat could be eaten. Those special offerings had to be taken outside the camp and completely burned to ashes.
